doc.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06

title: Lou Dillon the teacher and more modern players
summary: Suhor credits drummer Lou Dillon as a teacher who shaped Reed and himself and whose methods he used teaching Johnny Vidacovich; more names are listed.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Somebody I should mention just because he is sort of a grandparent-like link with so many of the players of the time is a drummer named Lou Dillon, who's now the retiring business agent. He was a damn good teacher. He played some jazz well, played Latin music, played show drums, a good show drummer. But he taught Reed Vaughn when Reed was just kind of bumping around trying to find a style. I know Lou. He's nice. Okay. Reed then said you've got to take lessons from this guy I'm taking from, because Reed was working, just working. You know, and so I went to Lou, a brilliant teacher, and the style of teaching that he did there was so conceptually strong, so encouraging, I think he opened things up for both Reed and me, and I used a lot of his methods when I taught Johnny Vodakovich in Another Generation. You know, so Lou is not known as one of your fire-eating players, but I think he had a lot of influence, at least on the drummers who heard Reed, who I came in contact with, and the drummers who I taught. But anyway, I don't, I mean, what can I say about modern players? John Probst, Joe Mandry, Mike Surpass, Don Seward, Dave West.
Rusty Main, who was an incredible player.

Yeah. But the list, I just wanted to get a sense of my view of who some of the leaders were, who people look to for innovation, you know, perhaps, again, your list might be different, Bill, but I wanted to get that on the table. Sure. Yours.
